headnote: Cal has taken a bus to the coast on his own. He is walking out along a sea wall to Saltmere, a place his nan has told him about for as long as he can remember.
text:
The bus went as far as the caravan park and stopped, because after that there is nowhere to turn round. From the shelter it was two miles of sea wall, with the marsh on my left going the colour of a bruise as the afternoon got on.

I had been meaning to walk out to Saltmere for about four years. Twice I had got as far as the caravan park.

Nan calls it the chapel, although there is no chapel on the map and no name printed anywhere near it. Her mother was born out there in a row of four cottages. By the time Nan was my age there were two of them left, and now there is a step that goes down into water and a piece of wall with the shape of a window in it. That is the story I have had all my life, told slightly differently each time. Some years the sea came in one night in February and took the lot. Some years it took forty years about it, a bit at a go, and everybody watched it happen and moved their furniture up the hill.

The photograph was the reason I was out there. Nan has been at Fern Court since March and there is nothing on her wall but a calendar from the surgery, so I said I would get her a picture of the place. I could not tell you which visit I said it on. She agrees with most things now, the way you agree with the radio.

I had told Mum I was going to Ryan's.

The wall is only a bank of earth with a path worn along the top of it, and the further out you go the less anybody has bothered with it. There were sheep on the landward side and hardly any grass for them. Below me a boat lay in the mud with its ribs showing through and a gull standing on it, and further along, a half mile of posts went out into the channel in a line, black and leaning, like the last of something that used to be a bridge.

About halfway along, the wind dropped out of my ears and I could hear how much water there was. It sat behind the bank on my right, shifting itself about, higher up than the field I was walking beside. I kept going and did not look over for a while.

The birds went up twice. Both times it was because of me.

Saltmere, when I got to it, was smaller than any version of the story. The step is there. The wall is there, about as high as a wheelie bin, with an elder growing out of the top and the window-shape you can put your arm through. Somebody had been out before me and left a can in the grass. I picked it up because it seemed rude not to, and then had nowhere to put it, so I carried it round with me, which spoiled the effect.

I stood on the step. The water came up over the toe of my boot and went out again. I moved back, and a minute later it came further up, and I understood it was not going to stop doing that for me.

Nan says you can hear the bell out there when the tide turns. I stood still long enough to be sure. There is a buoy in the channel that knocks when the water moves, a flat sound with nothing musical in it, and I decided that was what she had always meant, and that she knew it.

The light was going, and the marsh behind me had gone from bruise to no colour at all. I got the phone out. I had to hold it in both hands, and even then the picture came out grey and shaken along one edge where my hand had moved. It has the elder in it and about half the window. I have not sent it to anybody. I put the phone back in my pocket and started counting the posts the other way.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: a doctor's practice, which gives out free calendars
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The operation sense is the one most children reach for first and it actively misleads; the context supplies the British sense.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: the raised ridge of earth that holds the sea back
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: a place that keeps money; the edge of a river; to bank a fire
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Common word with a strong dominant sense pulling the wrong way, resolved only by the geography around it.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: the deep water route out beyond the mudflats
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: a television channel; a groove cut in something
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: Used twice in different sentences, and understanding it is needed to picture where the buoy is.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: the tide changing direction between coming in and going out
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: to turn round; a turn in a game; to turn into something
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: A specific coastal sense of a very ordinary verb, and it sets up the buoy that replaces the bell.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: wooden stakes driven into the mud in a line
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: letters delivered by the post; a job or position; to post a message
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The final image depends on it, and the competing senses are all high frequency.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: a small tree growing out of the top of the wall
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: an older person, or the older of two people
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The tree sense is uncommon in classrooms, and the surrounding verb 'growing' is the only clue.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: ruined the mood he had been trying to have
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: food that has gone off; a spoiled child; to spoil somebody with treats
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The word quietly admits Cal came out for an effect, so its sense here carries the complication.

wordVaultCandidates.senseInPassage: the feeling or impression the visit was making
wordVaultCandidates.otherCommonSense: a result — what something causes to happen
wordVaultCandidates.whyValuable: The result sense is the one a child owns and it is the sense the sentence does not want. Line 32 has a can spoiling something that cannot be a result, because a result is not the kind of thing a can in your hand spoils.

authoringRead.openingReference: FAULT, MILD, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT PROVES THE QUESTION IS ASKABLE ON A COMMISSIONED TEXT. Line 2 opens "From the shelter" — a definite article on first mention, with no shelter named anywhere before it. It is inferable from line 1, where the bus stops, and no child will be stopped by it. Recorded because the shape is exactly the shape the front-trim rule was written for, and it arrived here with no trim in sight: THE QUESTION IS ABOUT THE READER'S ENTRY POINT, NOT ABOUT CUTTING. Nothing else: Cal is the narrator and unnamed in the text, Nan is introduced at line 6, Mum at 17, and Saltmere at 4.
authoringRead.seams: VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION, and answered rather than skipped. A seam is created by joining two spans that were not adjacent in a source. This text has no source and no cuts, so there is no join anywhere in it and the question cannot have a yes. Recorded because an unanswered question and an unaskable one look identical on a passage record.
authoringRead.pronounResolution: VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION. The rule fires when a cut removes a paragraph naming a person, leaving the next paragraph's pronouns unresolved. Nothing was cut. Every person in this text is introduced by the text.
authoringRead.itemsLeanOn: CHECKED AGAINST ENG-009, TWELVE ITEMS. One thin anchor, recorded and not barred: SM-08 asks what he means by "the effect" at line 32. The text establishes it obliquely — line 28 has Saltmere smaller than any version of the story, and the can he cannot put down is the thing that spoils it — so the answer is available but it is the least directly stated key in the cluster. SM-09 is the subtlest: it needs the water at lines 33-35 read as the SLOW version of the two at lines 10-12, and a child who reads a minute-by-minute advance as fast will not get there. Sound, and the hardest item in the pair.
